clinicalPearls: Uterine prolapse is descent of the uterus and cervix into or beyond the vagina due to weakening of the pelvic floor supports, and it often coexists with prolapse of the vaginal walls, bladder, and rectum
Typical symptoms include a sensation of vaginal bulge or something coming down, pelvic heaviness or dragging, and symptoms that worsen through the day and with standing or straining
Associated urinary, bowel, and sexual dysfunction are common and should be assessed directly, as women may not volunteer them
Major risk factors include vaginal childbirth, increasing age and menopause, chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, chronic cough or constipation, and connective tissue laxity
Severity is graded by how far the leading part of the prolapse descends relative to the hymen, using a standardised staging system
Conservative management with pelvic floor muscle training and vaginal pessaries is appropriate for many women, particularly if surgery is undesirable or unsafe
Surgical options range from uterine-preserving procedures to hysterectomy with vault support, and the choice depends on symptoms, fertility wishes, and fitness
Vaginal oestrogen can improve atrophic tissue and support pessary use in postmenopausal women
reference.pathophysiology: The uterus and vagina are held in position by the levator ani muscles and the endopelvic fascia and ligaments, including the uterosacral and cardinal ligaments. Damage to these supports, most often from stretching and denervation during vaginal delivery, together with age-related and oestrogen-deficiency-related weakening of connective tissue and muscle, allows the pelvic organs to descend. Sustained increases in intra-abdominal pressure accelerate this process. As support fails, the uterus and cervix prolapse downward, frequently dragging the vaginal walls and adjacent bladder and rectum with them.
additionalDifferentials: Cystocele or rectocele without significant uterine descent
Large vaginal or cervical cyst or fibroid
Urethral diverticulum or other vaginal mass
additionalInvestigations: Pelvic examination in different positions and with straining to define the compartments and stage
Assessment of pelvic floor muscle strength
Urinary assessment including post-void residual and urodynamics where incontinence complicates management
Consideration of imaging for large or atypical masses
Evaluation and treatment of contributing factors such as constipation, chronic cough, and atrophy
redFlags: Ulceration, bleeding, or infection of exposed prolapsed tissue
Urinary retention or obstructed voiding from advanced prolapse
Hydronephrosis or renal impairment from ureteric kinking in severe procidentia
New abnormal bleeding requiring exclusion of malignancy
Complete procidentia that cannot be reduced, needing prompt specialist assessment
reference.prognosis: Uterine prolapse is a benign but often progressive quality-of-life condition; conservative measures relieve symptoms in many women, and surgery provides good results though prolapse can recur in other compartments over time. Prognosis is favourable overall, and attention to modifiable risk factors such as weight, constipation, and chronic cough helps limit progression and recurrence.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about associated urinary, bowel, and sexual symptoms
Overlooking coexisting prolapse in other vaginal compartments
Missing occult stress incontinence unmasked after prolapse correction
Neglecting to exclude malignancy in a woman with abnormal bleeding
Not treating vaginal atrophy or constipation that undermines pessary use and surgical outcomes
